title: Mobilisation within 24 hours of hip fracture surgery and prolonged hospital stay
subtitle: Case-control study sampled from the unit's hip fracture list
statement: About half of the 420 adults treated each year for hip fracture on the trauma unit are mobilised by a physiotherapist within 24 hours of surgery, against a national standard of the day after surgery. The unit wants to know whether early mobilisation is associated with shorter stays before asking for weekend physiotherapy cover. The exposure is recorded only in paper notes that take about 25 minutes each to read, and the published evidence conflicts once confounding by how unwell patients are is taken into account.
whoAffected: Adults with hip fracture on the trauma unit, most of them older and many with dementia; their families; physiotherapists and ward staff; the hospital planning weekend cover.
whatHurts: Long stays bring deconditioning, delirium and hospital-acquired infection and delay return home; asking for weekend cover without evidence risks spending on staff that may not shorten stays.
currentPractice: First mobilisation within 24 hours for about half of patients; no physiotherapy at weekends; delays documented in handwritten notes before 2025.
whyNow: The service planning round in April 2027 will consider weekend therapy cover, and 100 hours of note reading are approved this winter.
constraints: About 100 hours of clerical and physiotherapy time for reading notes; paper notes for 2022 to 2024 only; no contact with patients; results needed for the service planning round in April 2027.
patientCenteredGoal: Patients with hip fracture get up and walking as soon as it is safe and go home without avoidable weeks in hospital.
summary: Problem framed as a case-control study of early mobilisation and prolonged stay, with confounding as the central difficulty.
